summary: Supply the target horsepower at crankshaft, number of cylinders, the max duty cycle and the Flow rate 1 and the Fuel injector calculator solves for target horsepower at wheels. It is built for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Fuel injector calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fuel injector calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports target horsepower at wheels in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the aspiration); then you type in the target horsepower at crankshaft, number of cylinders, the max duty cycle and the Flow rate 1.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fuel injector calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Target horsepower at wheels=(20 ÷ 23) × target horsepower at crankshaft
Fuel pressure=435000 × (Bsfc 1 ^ 2) × (target horsepower at crankshaft ^ 2) ÷ ((number of cylinders ^ 2) × (max duty cycle ^ 2) × (Flow rate 1 ^ 2))
Fuel pressure=435000 × (Bsfc 2 ^ 2) × (target horsepower at crankshaft ^ 2) ÷ ((number of cylinders ^ 2) × (max duty cycle ^ 2) × (Flow rate 2 ^ 2))
Bsfc 3=(1 ÷ 8700) × the square root of (174) × number of cylinders × max duty cycle × Flow rate 3 ÷ (target horsepower at crankshaft × the square root of (1 ÷ fuel pressure))
Flow rate 1 cc=(21 ÷ 2) × flow rate1
Flow rate 2=(2 ÷ 21) × Flow rate 2 cc

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Pressure, opening in bars

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fuel injector calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the target horsepower at crankshaft, number of cylinders and the max duty cycle — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Fuel injector calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns target horsepower at wheels, derived from the target horsepower at crankshaft, number of cylinders and the max duty cycle. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fuel injector calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the target horsepower at crankshaft, number of cylinders, the max duty cycle and the flow rate1, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter fuel pressure in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Fuel pressure opens in bars and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Bsfc 1 = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Fuel injector calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
